newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee surges, but rally dented by late sale.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee surges, but rally dented by late sale.

text.p: Eleventh-hour sell-off knocked London's robusta coffee futures from their peak on Wednesday but prices still finished at new nine-month highs after chasing a fresh New York rally.

London's benchmark May breached the $1,800-mark to hit a session high of $1,820 a tonne, up by seven percent on the day, after New York's May futures sailed through the closely-watched $2.00/lb hurdle, the highest level since the damaging Brazilian frosts in 1994.
But aggressive profit-taking soon pulled the contract back to below $1,800, closing the day $82 up at $1,780, the highest since last June.
"There was profit-taking right on the closing bell," said one. "If you are long of the market and you see a rise of $100 what are you going to do. Are you going to hold it?"
"It's a short term market at the moment. London has to keep tracking New York to a certain extent," he said. The market's advance earlier in the day was capped by Indonesian and Vietnam selling.
Recent reports of coffee shipment delays or origin defaults from Vietnam have helped buoy sentiment in London.
But the prime mover in New York is concern of a March squeeze ahead of expiry later this month as there is still very little certified coffee to meet delivery.
Recent news of supply disruptions from Central American origins and forecasts of lower 1997/98 Brazilian harvest did little to soothe the market's nerves.
"This is the epitomy of a bull market. Whatever news comes out it's going to be regarded as bullish news," said one trader.
While traders said there would be continued supply tightness well into the second half of this year, some roasters said they would not start panic buying although the pressure is rising.
The roasting industry had stepped up buying after the market began to stir since early this year. But some analysts warned that the explosive rally if persisted could cool down retail demand.

"The supply situation is not that bad," said London-based coffee analyst Kerry Muir. "Prices may be held up to the present level otherwise there will be nasty spiral down effect from lower consumption again."
